title: Gabriella Angelica Jemima Hasian
text: Hi, I’m Gabriella Hasian, a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia with a background in Actuarial Science and several years of experience in credit decisioning. Before pursuing my MDS, I worked in banking, where I focused on using data and analytics to support credit risk and portfolio management. This experience sparked my interest in applying data science to real-world problems and using data to drive better decisions. I’m now looking to deepen my expertise in data science and explore opportunities at the intersection of data, technology, and finance.

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
text:
This analysis examines fuel efficiency in the mtcars dataset while demonstrating how R and Python can work together within the same Quarto document. R is used to prepare the data and calculate average fuel efficiency by cylinder group. The resulting R objects are then passed to Python for further analysis and visualization. Finally, a result calculated in Python is passed back to R.
The mtcars dataset contains fuel consumption and other characteristics of 32 automobiles. The dataset is included in R’s datasets package and was originally extracted from the 1974 issue of Motor Trend magazine.
Data source: R datasets package — mtcars documentation:
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/mtcars.html

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
text:
Setting Up R and Python
I use reticulate to connect R and Python within the same Quarto document. Python is configured to use the project’s .venv environment so that the same environment used by the rest of the project is used during rendering.

library(tidyverse)
library(reticulate)

use_virtualenv("../../.venv", required = TRUE)

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
text:
Preparing the Data in R
I begin with the built-in mtcars dataset in R. I move the car names from the row names into a regular column and convert the number of cylinders into a categorical variable. This makes the cylinder groups easier to compare in the analysis.

mtcars_data <- mtcars |>
  rownames_to_column("model") |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl))

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
section: Calculating Fuel Efficiency by Cylinder Group in R
text:
Calculating Fuel Efficiency by Cylinder Group in R
I calculate the average miles per gallon (mpg) and number of cars for each cylinder group.
The resulting r_summary object is calculated entirely in R and will be passed to Python in the next section.

r_summary <- mtcars_data |>
  group_by(cyl) |>
  summarise(
    mean_mpg = mean(mpg),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    mean_mpg = round(mean_mpg, 2)
  )

r_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  cyl   mean_mpg     n
  <fct>    <dbl> <int>
1 4         26.7    11
2 6         19.7     7
3 8         15.1    14


The results show how average fuel efficiency differs across the cylinder groups. I now pass this R object to Python for further analysis.

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
text:
Using R Objects in Python
The r object provided by reticulate allows Python to access objects created in R. Here, Python receives both the car-level dataset and the summary calculated in R.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

python_data = r.mtcars_data
python_summary = r.r_summary

python_summary

  cyl  mean_mpg   n
0   4     26.66  11
1   6     19.74   7
2   8     15.10  14


The python_summary object is therefore not independently created in Python. It is the r_summary object that was calculated in R and passed into the Python session.

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
section: Identifying the Highest-Fuel-Efficiency Group in Python
text:
Identifying the Highest-Fuel-Efficiency Group in Python
I use Python to identify the cylinder group with the highest average fuel efficiency.

top_cyl = python_summary.loc[
    python_summary["mean_mpg"].idxmax(),
    "cyl"
]

top_mpg = python_summary["mean_mpg"].max()

print("Cylinder group with the highest mean MPG:", top_cyl)

Cylinder group with the highest mean MPG: 4

print("Highest mean MPG:", top_mpg)

Highest mean MPG: 26.66


The Python calculation identifies the cylinder group with the highest average MPG. The resulting top_cyl object will now be passed back to R.

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
section: Passing the Python Result Back to R
text:
Passing the Python Result Back to R
The py object provided by reticulate allows R to access objects created in Python. I use py$top_cyl to retrieve the result calculated by Python.

top_cyl_from_python <- py$top_cyl

top_cyl_from_python

[1] "4"


This demonstrates the two-way exchange of objects between the two languages:
R object → Python → Python result → R

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
text:
Visualizing Fuel Efficiency in Python
The following visualization uses the car-level data originally prepared in R and passed to Python as python_data.
The x-axis represents vehicle weight, while the y-axis represents fuel efficiency. Point size represents horsepower, and the legend distinguishes cars by cylinder group. Individual car names are also labelled to make the observations identifiable.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

for cyl in sorted(python_data["cyl"].unique()):
    subset = python_data[python_data["cyl"] == cyl]

    _ = ax.scatter(
        subset["wt"],
        subset["mpg"],
        s=subset["hp"] * 1.8,
        alpha=0.75,
        label=f"{int(cyl)} cylinders",
    )

    for _, row in subset.iterrows():
        _ = ax.annotate(
            row["model"],
            (row["wt"], row["mpg"]),
            xytext=(5, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
            fontsize=7,
            alpha=0.8,
        )

_ = ax.set_xlabel("Vehicle weight (1000 lbs)")
_ = ax.set_ylabel("Fuel efficiency (MPG)")
_ = ax.set_title("Vehicle Weight vs. Fuel Efficiency")
_ = ax.legend(title="Cylinder group")
_ = ax.grid(alpha=0.2)

_ = plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Vehicle weight and fuel efficiency across cars, with point size representing horsepower and cylinder group represented by the legend





The visualization shows the relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency while providing additional information about horsepower and cylinder group. The data used for the plot originated in R and was passed to Python through reticulate.

title: Fuel Efficiency Analysis of Cars Using R and Python
text:
Conclusion
This analysis demonstrates how R and Python can be combined within a single Quarto document using reticulate.
R was used to prepare the mtcars dataset and calculate average MPG by cylinder group. The resulting r_summary object was passed from R to Python using r.r_summary. Python then used this object to identify the cylinder group with the highest average MPG.
The Python result was subsequently passed back to R using py$top_cyl. Python was also used to visualize the car-level data that had originally been prepared in R.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Catching sunsets between assignments


Starting the Master of Data Science at UBC has been an exciting experience so far. Orientation was a great opportunity to meet my classmates and get a sense of what the next few months would look like. Coming from Indonesia and starting this new chapter in Vancouver, it was exciting—and a little overwhelming—to suddenly be surrounded by people from different backgrounds and experiences.
The first weeks of classes have been fast-paced, with a lot to learn and even more to keep up with. What surprised me most was how quickly we moved from introductions to actually working with data, programming, and new concepts. I’m enjoying the challenge, especially seeing how different everyone’s approaches can be when solving the same problem.
I’m still getting used to the pace and finding my routine, but I’m feeling excited about what’s ahead. There is definitely a lot to learn, but I’m looking forward to making the most of the MDS experience, both inside and outside the classroom.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass with Python
text:
Cleaning the data
The variables used in this analysis are species, flipper length, and body mass. I remove observations that are missing values for these variables.

analysis_data = penguins[
    ["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
].dropna()

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass with Python
text:
Comparing body mass across species
Next, I calculate the average and median body mass for each penguin species.

summary = (
    analysis_data
    .groupby("species")["body_mass_g"]
    .agg(["count", "mean", "median"])
    .round(1)
)

The summary shows how typical body mass differs among the three species.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass with Python
section: Relationship between flipper length and body mass
text:
Relationship between flipper length and body mass
Finally, I visualize the relationship between flipper length and body mass.

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))

for species, group in analysis_data.groupby("species"):
    plt.scatter(
        group["flipper_length_mm"],
        group["body_mass_g"],
        label=species,
        alpha=0.7
    )

plt.xlabel("Flipper length (mm)")
plt.ylabel("Body mass (g)")
plt.title("Flipper Length and Body Mass by Penguin Species")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Relationship between flipper length and body mass across penguin species





The plot shows a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass: penguins with longer flippers generally tend to have greater body mass. The species also occupy somewhat different regions of the plot, suggesting that species is associated with differences in these physical measurements.

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass with R
text:
Cleaning the data
The variables used in this analysis are species, flipper length, and body mass. I remove observations that are missing values for these variables.

analysis_data <- penguins |>
  select(species, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g) |>
  drop_na()

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass with R
text:
Comparing body mass across species
Next, I calculate the average and median body mass for each penguin species.

summary <- analysis_data |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean = mean(body_mass_g),
    median = median(body_mass_g)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1)))

summary

title: Exploring Penguin Body Mass with R
section: Relationship between flipper length and body mass
text:
Relationship between flipper length and body mass
Finally, I visualize the relationship between flipper length and body mass.

ggplot(analysis_data, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, color = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between Flipper Length and Body Mass",
    x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The plot shows a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass. Penguins with longer flippers generally have greater body mass. The three species also form somewhat distinct groups, with Gentoo penguins generally having both longer flippers and higher body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

title: About
text: I grew up in Jakarta, Indonesia, as the firstborn in my family. I have always been drawn to quantitative thinking and curious about how numbers and data can be used to understand and solve problems. As data became increasingly important across industries, I began my career in banking, where I worked on credit decisioning and encountered real-world challenges involving backtesting, data management, and analytics. I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to learn and apply these concepts in an industry setting before returning to school to deepen my knowledge and explore data science from a broader perspective.

title: About
text:
Why Data Science
My experience in banking and the boost of data usage that currently growing made me increasingly curious about what could be done beyond traditional analysis. I wanted to strengthen my ability to work with data, build analytical solutions, and approach problems from a more computational perspective which still applicable in the industry. This led me to pursue the Master of Data Science at UBC. I hope to expand my technical skills and explore new ways of applying data science to meaningful problems and see things from different perspectives.

title: About
text:
Outside of Data Science
Outside of school and work, I enjoy travelling, exploring new places, and trying different foods. When I’m away from the screen, I often find myself reading a book on the balcony and enjoying some fresh air. I also try to stay active and make time for activities that help me maintain a good balance between work and personal life. As I begin this new chapter in Vancouver, I’m looking forward to exploring the city and experiencing all that it has to offer.
